clue.text: Fly — or endlessly, repeatedly to sea

indicators.note: without their ends: each of the two words here drops its final letter
the shortened block is given again, so it appears twice in a row

parts.note: the two words taken as written, each time

explanation.surface: An instruction to a fly, or a sailor, to head out to sea over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts the last letter from each of 'to' and 'sea', leaving T and SE, so TSE; 'repeatedly' doubles it.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsetse is an African biting insect that carries sleeping sickness, so it is a kind of fly.

clue.text: Traditional number of herbs?

definitions.meaning: a 'number' in the music trade is a song, and a traditional one is a folk tune with no known author
not a count of them: the herbs are the four the refrain lists, parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark carries the whole clue. Scarborough Fair is an English folk ballad, and its herb-listing refrain is probably the best-known line in the tradition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad's refrain runs 'parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme', so a folk song that lists herbs describes this title and no other.

clue.text: What may be taken from Raptor on tour somewhere in Ontario

indicators.note: Taking something from a phrase means lifting letters that are already sitting in it, in the order they were written.

parts.note: seven consecutive letters straddle all three words, beginning inside the first

explanation.surface: A question about what a touring bird of prey might carry off from a stop somewhere in Ontario.
explanation.walkthrough: The Raptors are Toronto's basketball team, so the city is sitting inside a phrase about its own side travelling — the surface names the answer twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: Ontario is a Canadian province and Toronto its largest city, so the definition points at the answer as one place among several it could mean.

clue.text: Penning rubbish long since

indicators.note: To rubbish a thing is to trash it, and letters that have been trashed do not stay in the order they arrived in.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.surface: A writer has been churning out drivel for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'rubbish' as a noun and the clue is a complaint about old junk; read it as a verb and it is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To pen animals is to shut them in a fenced space, which is the sense the answer carries; the writing sense of 'pen' is the decoy.

clue.text: Brothers who may give prior approval

definitions.meaning: the men who head a monastery are members of its brotherhood, monks like the rest of them
a prior is the deputy who runs a monastery under its head, so approving one is a job for the rank above

explanation.walkthrough: 'Prior approval' is the sort of phrase a form asks for, which is the misdirection: the prior here is a person, a monastery's second in command, and the approval is his superior's.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbot is the elected head of an abbey, a monk among monks and the rank immediately above a prior, so both halves name the same office.

clue.text: On social media, befriended a journalist bored by Double Dutch

indicators.note: bored by means the pair drills into the middle of the first part

parts.note: ED, short for editor, stands for a journalist
Double asks for the Dutch abbreviation a second time

explanation.surface: Someone online adds a journalist friend who is bored by gibberish.
explanation.walkthrough: Double Dutch is gibberish, but here it is D twice, inside A + ED.
explanation.definitionFit: On social platforms such as Facebook, to add someone is to accept them as a friend or contact.

clue.text: Continue to divulge secrets, overheard in city of sin

indicators.note: overheard means caught by ear, so the phrase is said aloud and spelt as a different word

parts.note: to babble on is to keep talking and let things slip

explanation.surface: Someone keeps spilling secrets, overheard in a wicked city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overheard' tells you that BABBLE ON, said aloud, gives the spelling of the ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: Babylon is the biblical byword for a decadent, corrupt city, the 'great harlot' of Revelation.

clue.text: A larger squat, far off in London location

indicators.note: Milk goes off when it will no longer hold together, and letters that have gone off will not hold their order either.

parts.note: fifteen letters of fodder, taken exactly as they stand

explanation.surface: Squatters have taken over a bigger building somewhere across London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A larger squat, far off' reads as a description of an illegal occupation somewhere distant, and only the last word of it is an instruction; the other five are raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the plaza at the centre of the capital, with Nelson's Column in the middle, so the definition names it by category and city.

clue.text: A supporter twice defending scoundrel, it might be said — for a spell

definitions.text: it might be said — for a spell

indicators.note: defending means the pair surrounds the scoundrel like guards

parts.note: a bra is a supporting garment
twice asks for A plus the supporter a second time
a cad is a scoundrel

explanation.surface: Someone backs a rogue twice over, as if casting a spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it might be said' tells you the answer is a word spoken aloud by a magician, not a description of a spell.
explanation.definitionFit: Abracadabra is the word a conjuror says when casting a spell.

clue.text: Vacuous 'gagster', Everyman's leaving you stony-faced

indicators.note: Something vacuous is empty in the middle, so the word beside it keeps only the letters at its two ends.

parts.note: hollow out the joker's word and its first and last letters are what is left
this paper's setter signs himself Everyman, so his own 'I am' contracts to two letters

explanation.surface: The setter admits a brainless comedian is leaving you unamused.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the name this crossword's setter writes under, and 'Everyman's' is him saying I'm — a signature trick worth knowing, because he uses himself as fodder most weeks.
explanation.definitionFit: Grim describes a face set hard and unsmiling, the look of someone braced for bad news, which is what a stony expression is.

clue.text: What has holy musician turned out?

definitions.text: What has holy musician turned out?
definitions.note: An &lit: the whole question defines the answer, and two of its words hand over their outer letters at the same time.

indicators.note: You turn out a pocket or a drawer by emptying it, so each word named keeps only the letters at its edges.

parts.note: empty the middle of the word and its first and last letters stay put
the same treatment for the player: outside letters kept, the six inside dropped

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a devout composer has produced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' does double duty: in the surface it means produced, in the wordplay it means emptied, which is why the clue is true read either way.
explanation.definitionFit: A hymn is a song of praise written for worship, precisely what a religious musician produces, so the question reads as a straight definition.

clue.text: One in the green helping those in the red?

definitions.meaning: the outlaw of the ballads wore Lincoln green and lived in the greenwood of Sherwood Forest
to be in the red is to be in debt, and this man took from the rich and handed it to the poor

explanation.walkthrough: Two colours and two idioms: Lincoln green is what the legend wore, being in the red is owing money, and the modern banking phrase is put to medieval work.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the greenwood outlaw of English legend who robbed the rich to pay the poor, so both halves point at the same figure.

clue.text: LSD enthusiast allegedly revolutionising youth in their heads?

definitions.text: LSD enthusiast allegedly revolutionising youth in their heads?
definitions.note: An &lit: every word of the sentence describes the man, and the same words hand over their opening letters.

indicators.note: The head of a word is its opening letter, so this asks for the first letter of each word that has gone before.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the five words, read in the order given

explanation.surface: Rumour has it an acid-loving guru was turning young minds upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: Timothy Leary was the Harvard psychologist sacked over his LSD experiments, who told the sixties to turn on and drop out — so the sentence is a fair description as well as a recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: Leary preached LSD to the young in the sixties, so the sentence describes the man and doubles as the instruction that spells his name.

clue.text: Study hard about … about … primarily Italian … Italian engineer

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to cram is to study hard before an exam
on means about, as in a book on birds

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so take the opening letter

parts.note: its first letter is I

explanation.surface: A halting note about cramming, about something mainly Italian, about an Italian engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'about's do different jobs: the first turns CRAM round to MARC, the second means ON, as in a talk on a subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Guglielmo Marconi was the Italian inventor and electrical engineer who pioneered long-distance radio transmission.

clue.text: Kingpin mixed drink

indicators.note: A mixed drink is stirred together out of separate parts, and letters treated that way lose the order they came in.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder: the boss of the outfit, taken as one word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed drink' is a phrase you read as a unit, which is what hides the seam: 'mixed' belongs to the word in front of it, and 'drink' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: It is gin with a dash of Angostura bitters, a naval officers' tipple, so the definition is the plain category the answer belongs to.

clue.text: His dishonesty increases the bill

definitions.meaning: not a restaurant scam: the lying itself sets the change off, and the change happens to the liar
a bill is a beak, and by extension a nose, so what grows is a face rather than a total

explanation.walkthrough: Pinocchio's nose lengthens every time he lies, which is the picture behind the pun, and 'bill' is the pivot: a restaurant total in the surface, a beak in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the puppet whose nose grows with each lie, so a lengthening 'bill' — a beak — is exactly what his lying produces.

clue.text: Accommodation husband finding stimulating — run away

indicators.note: the run letter is taken away from the stimulating word

parts.note: rousing means stirring or stimulating
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A husband finds a place stimulating, then runs off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run away' reads as fleeing, but 'run' is the cricket abbreviation and 'away' removes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Housing is accommodation, the provision of homes for people.

clue.text: In hearing, ne'er-do-well is to improve

definitions.note: heal is used intransitively, as in wounds heal, meaning get better

indicators.note: in hearing means as spoken out loud, so the scoundrel's word is said and a matching word spelt

parts.note: a heel is a contemptible, untrustworthy person

explanation.surface: A judge says that, at a court hearing, a ne'er-do-well is to reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In hearing' looks like a court hearing, but it tells you HEEL is said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: To heal is to get better or recover, which is what improving in health means.

clue.text: Imminent aperçu

definitions.meaning: split after two letters, the phrase says a thing is near enough to be seen coming
a French loanword for a brief flash of understanding, a glimpse into how something works

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the giveaway: (2,5) says two words, and only one of the two meanings needs the gap. Seven letters do both jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it means close at hand; read as one it is a sudden grasp of how a thing works, which is what an aperçu is.

clue.text: With head cleared, migraine treated somewhere in W Africa

indicators.note: the remaining letters are worked on and rearranged, as a doctor treats a patient
the head, the first letter, is removed from migraine

explanation.surface: A migraine is treated and the head clears somewhere in West Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head cleared' sounds like relief from the migraine, but it removes the word's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigeria is a large country on the west African coast, by the Gulf of Guinea.

clue.text: Criminals and perjurer throwing off tail: some nerve!

parts.note: a gang is a group of criminals

indicators.note: the tail, the last letter, is dropped from the liar

parts.note: a perjurer lies under oath, so is a liar

explanation.surface: Crooks and a lying witness show some cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some nerve!' sounds like an exclamation at cheek, but it means some nerve tissue.
explanation.definitionFit: Ganglia are clusters of nerve cells, so they form part of the nervous system.

clue.text: Fires X and Y?

definitions.meaning: to axe a job or the person doing it is to cut them, the verb every headline uses for redundancies
the two reference lines of a graph are labelled with exactly those letters

explanation.walkthrough: Two plurals with nothing in common: one is a verb for sacking people, the other the pair of lines you plot a graph against. The question mark flags definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: To axe staff is to fire them, and the X and Y lines of a graph carry the same name — two unrelated senses of one short word.

clue.text: Causes of discomfort hidden in tea chest

indicators.note: Something hidden in a phrase is already there in plain letters, waiting to be read straight out of the middle of it.

parts.note: five consecutive letters bridge the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Something painful has been stowed away in a wooden packing crate.
explanation.walkthrough: A tea chest is the plywood box tea was shipped in, a real thing rather than a random pairing, and that is what makes the surface sit still enough to hide letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An ache is a dull, lingering pain, and a pain is precisely a cause of discomfort, so the plural phrase suits the plural answer.

clue.text: Method with which you prepare the quince

indicators.note: Preparing a fruit means cutting it up before it goes in the pan, and letters prepared that way do not stay whole.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, the article included

explanation.surface: A cookery book explains how to get a quince ready for the pan.
explanation.walkthrough: A quince is a hard, sour fruit that has to be cooked before it is edible, so 'prepare the quince' reads as a recipe line and hides the instruction in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A technique is a settled way of doing something, which is what a method is: a plain synonym, noun for noun, with no stretch in it.

clue.text: Mechanically produces seat for cycling

indicators.note: Letters go round a loop: the one at the front is carried to the back and every other letter keeps its place in the queue.

parts.note: a stool is a backless seat, five letters ready to be rotated

explanation.surface: A factory machine turns out saddles for bicycles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat for cycling' pictures a bicycle saddle, and that is the trap: the last word is not describing the seat, it is telling you what to do with its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To tool a part is to shape it with machinery, so the definition is the verb sense of a word everybody knows as a noun.

clue.text: At first, Aston Villa (without No 1) hoping to animate emotion of England fans

indicators.note: At first means only the opening letter of Aston

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to animate means to stir these letters into life in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: without No 1 means Villa loses its first letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Aston Villa, an English football club, without its top player, hoping to stir up fans of England.
explanation.walkthrough: A comes first; then the letters of HOPING plus ILLA (Villa without V) are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglophilia is a love of England and things English, the feeling of its admirers.

clue.text: Good: musical instrument's flipping free

indicators.note: To flip a thing is to turn it over end for end, so the letters just named are read the other way round.

parts.note: the Indian long-necked lute is a sitar, and turned over it reads backwards
the standard one-letter abbreviation, as on a school report

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted that a musical instrument is being given away at no charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is also the mild expletive an exasperated speaker reaches for, which is what keeps the surface sounding like a sentence about a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratis means at no charge, the Latin-derived word a notice uses when it wants the sense of costing nothing rather than of being unconfined.

clue.text: Speechified, valued by none

parts.note: nothing is written as a nought, and a nought on the page is the letter O
to rate a thing is to put a value on it

explanation.surface: Someone gave a speech that nobody thought much of.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a slight — a speech nobody thought much of — and the two halves are simply laid end to end, with 'by' doing nothing but joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to make a formal speech, usually a pompous one, so the past tense answers 'speechified' in both tone and inflection.
